The practice entails the use of sub-hallucinogenic doses of psychedelics substances such as LSD and psilocybin mushrooms. Users report a multiplicity of motivations for and benefits from engaging with microdosing that run across the enhancement/therapy continuum. At the same time, scientific research remains limited and inconclusive as to microdosing’s safety and effectiveness. Methods: The present paper draws on an extended, in-depth interview with a user of psychedelic microdosing to investigate key aspects pertaining to the practice. Results: The discussion focuses on the participant’s engagement with different substances, their understandings of the various risks potentially involved in microdosing, and how they manage these risks. Conclusion: The themes that emerge as significant out of these discussions relate to authenticity, identity and the broader dynamic and antagonisms between the world of psychedelics and dominant culture.

title: Risk-Aware Infrastructure Forecasting for Early Childhood Capacity: A Hybrid Demographic-Housing Model with Algorithmic Governance
abstract: This study presents a hybrid demographic-housing forecasting pipeline for preschool infrastructure demand in Singapore, designed for the Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA). The model integrates cohort-component population aging with Build-To-Order (BTO) housing delivery signals and Census 2020 subzone-specific child-per-unit ratios, replacing fixed national coefficients that introduce up to 10% estimation error (Wilson et al., 2021). OLS regression models the population-to-child-count relationship (R^2=0.87), while Monte Carlo simulation (n=1,000) transforms deterministic point-estimates into probabilistic planning ranges, establishing a 95th percentile confidence bound recommending a three-center national safety buffer. The pipeline embeds algorithmic governance tripwires — automated buffer-consumption thresholds at 25%, 50%, and 100% — that mandate escalating executive intervention before fiscal floors are breached (NIST, 2023). A Social Return on Investment (SROI) reconciliation maps pedagogical outcomes across five weighted domains to the Heckman Equation, adopting a conservative 1.75x social return estimate (Heckman et al., 2010). Break-even analysis identifies a 3.5-month fiscal inflection point with a 4.62-month margin of safety for construction acceleration investments. Keywords: Infrastructure Planning, Early Childhood Education, Demographic Forecasting, Algorithmic Governance, Monte Carlo Simulation, Urban Analytics, Singapore Housing

title: Productive Policy Competition and Asymmetric Extremism
abstract: Viable policies must be developed by individuals and groups with the expertise and willingness to do so. We develop a model in which competing policy-motivated developers differ in their intrinsic ideological extremism and ability at crafting high quality policies. The unique equilibrium exhibits unequal participation, inefficiently unpredictable and extreme policies and outcomes, wasted effort, and an apparent advantage for extreme policies. While asymmetries between the developers always reduce observable competition, they can nevertheless benefit the decisionmaker. This contrasts starkly with the classic all-pay contest -- where the decisionmaker is always harmed by asymmetries due to the discouragement effect -- and results from the developers' policy motivations. I also introduce and solve a broader class of generalized policy contests that nests both the policy-development model and the all-pay contest, and develop new methods for solving asymmetric contests with spillovers. Broadly, my analysis provides a novel rationale for why extreme actors may dominate policymaking that is rooted in the nature of policy development, and highlights the difficulty in assessing the normative implications of such dominance.

title: Violence and International Migration in Illiberal Times: The Case of El Salvador’s Authoritarian Transformation
abstract: Across a new transnational wave of illiberal governance, tough-on-crime approaches to public safety and migration are growing. The case of El Salvador, in which President Nayib Bukele suspended due process protections and imprisoned suspected gang members in mass beginning in late March 2022 under a State of Exception policy, offers a window into this process. Turning to a combination of administrative datasets and cross-national surveys, we show that despite tremendous public approval for President Bukele’s strategies as the solution to a long history of persistent gang violence and international migration, violence largely reduced before he implemented the State of Exception, and Salvadorans’ migration intentions have not declined. Moreover, we find no evidence that the policy or Bukele taking office produced a particular reduction in Salvadoran migration to either the U.S. or Mexico compared to Guatemalan and Honduran migration. Nor do we uncover clear evidence that return migration to El Salvador uniquely increased, undercutting conclusions that illiberal tough-on-crime policies like El Salvador’s are likely to address “root causes” of international migration.

title: The English Education System in the 16th- and 17th-centuries: Philanthropy and the Study of Science
abstract: This article continues the topic of the reform of education in 17th-century England from the paper ‘Literacy and the education system in 16th- and 17th -century England’, published as preprint on this site in January 2026 (DOI: 10.31235/osf.io/zfs7r_v1). Gresham College and London as the 'third university' in England are the themes.

title: The Non-Binarity of Artificial Intelligence Global Competition: 2018-2025
authors: Wiebke Dorfs, Maximilian Hampel, Joanna J. Bryson
abstract: Technological progress plays a crucial role in international relations. In particular, innovation has long been theorized as instrumental to power transitions. It is therefore unsurprising that the return of China as a global superpower and its technological advances has triggered considerable discussion. One narrative that has emerged is that of a binary "AI Cold War" competition between China and the US, similar to the 1947-1991 competition between nuclear superpowers. Another though is that the digital and information revolutions should facilitate technology and therefore power diffusion. Here we examine the claim of a binary competition, examining the state and trajectory of global AI competition for the years 2018, 2019, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025. We use AI patents defended globally in the WIPO database and the market capitalization of the companies holding them as proxies for innovation and market power. We find that the binary narrative underestimates the strength of other actors globally, notably but not exclusively the European Union and Japan. These are comparable to China, and on the innovation metric with the US. In terms of market power, the US is a significant outlier, with an order of magnitude more capital concentration. Our research therefore indicates that any binary AI cold war narrative is not data-led.

title: From Himalayan Catastrophe to National Resilience: Lessons from the 2026 Bhote Koshi and Trishuli River Floods in Nepal
abstract: The August 2026 Bhote Koshi–Trishuli disaster was not simply another flood. It was a cascading cryosphere disaster linking glacier instability, steep Himalayan topography, hydropower, highways, international trade, tourism, and pilgrimage—exposing weaknesses in transboundary observation, monitoring, and development planning (ICIMOD, 2026b; Reuters, 2026a). Nepal must treat it as a turning point. On the morning of 26 August 2026, the mountains above Nepal’s northern frontier delivered a disaster of almost unimaginable speed and scale. A massive mass of ice, rock, and sediment detached in the high Himalayan terrain near the Nepal–Tibet border, descended roughly 1,200 metres, interacted with the Lhende Khola system, and generated a debris-rich flood that surged through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river corridors, destroying settlements, markets, roads, bridges, hydropower facilities, and an international border crossing and transforming them into fields of mud, boulders, and wreckage within minutes (ICIMOD, 2026b; Reuters, 2026a). Satellite analysis indicates that a substantial section of glacier and adjoining rock detached from approximately 5,200 metres elevation, while river levels downstream rose by as much as seven to nine metres within approximately half an hour in some locations (ICIMOD, 2026b; The Guardian, 2026). That rate left extraordinarily little time for people to recognize the danger, much less to evacuate. Although some areas were warned via police megaphones, announcements by the local governments, and mobile alerts, most people took it as regular seasonal flood warnings and missed the opportunity to escape.

title: Religious Leaders and Distributive Politics in Postwar Italy
abstract: How do unelected local leaders shape distributive politics? Religious authorities and other local leaders are often deeply embedded in the communities that receive public investment, yet many have no formal role in allocating or delivering state resources. I argue that such leaders can nonetheless shape distribution by increasing electoral returns to public investment. I test this argument using data on public works from a large-scale development program in postwar Southern Italy, exploiting variation in the election of Christian Democratic (DC) politicians and the local embeddedness of Catholic bishops. Difference-in-differences estimates show that DC politicians allocate more public works where bishops are locally embedded. These investments translate into higher DC vote shares specifically where bishops are local, with no evidence that bishops lobby for community- or Church-aligned projects or are rewarded for prior electoral support. These findings shed new light on the relationship between political intermediation and distributive politics.

title: From Reach to Relationship: Reframing Social Media Recruitment as an Action Research Practice
abstract: Social media is routine infrastructure for participant recruitment in health and social research, yet methodological discussions typically evaluate platforms by reach, cost, speed, targeting, and conversion. This paper reframes social media recruitment through an action-research lens, positioning recruitment as an early site where participation is constituted, relationships begin, power is negotiated, and learning occurs. Drawing on a critical integrative review of 22 empirical and methodological studies addressing Facebook/Meta, Instagram, X/Twitter, Reddit, WhatsApp, WeChat, and multiplatform recruitment, we examine the affordances and relational tensions of digitally mediated recruitment. Social media can reduce costs, accelerate access to dispersed and stigmatized populations, and enable iterative adaptation, but can also reproduce sampling inequalities, platform surveillance, algorithmic governance, hostile interactions, fraud, and verification labour. We introduce recruitment-as-inquiry: the proposition that recruitment helps constitute the participatory field rather than merely populate it. We propose six interconnected practices: co-defining recruitment purpose; selecting platforms with communities; treating invitations as relational encounters; reflexively examining participation, absence, and exclusion; protecting integrity without undermining trust; and returning recruitment learning to subsequent inquiry and action. This framework extends action research upstream, aligning digital recruitment with its democratic, relational, reflexive, and transformative commitments.

title: Decreased Support for Political Violence in the United States in Mid-2026: Findings from a Nationally Representative Survey
authors: Garen Wintemute, Sonia Robinson, Krista Neumann, Daniel Tancredi, Shaina Sta Cruz, Aaron Shev, Elizabeth A. Tomsich, Bradley Velasquez, Mona A. Wright, Veronica Pear
abstract: Background: Recent survey research has found concerning but stable prevalences of support for and willingness to engage in political violence in the United States (US). This study re-estimates those prevalences in mid-2026—a midterm election year in which support for political violence might be expected to increase. Methods: Findings are from Wave 5, conducted May 15-June 15, 2026, of a nationally representative annual longitudinal survey of adult members of the Ipsos KnowledgePanel that was initiated in 2022. Primary findings are for the entire cohort; a secondary analysis examined responses by political party and Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement affiliations. Principal outcomes are measures of justification for, willingness to engage in, and anticipated firearm use in political violence. Results for individual years are presented as weighted prevalences and item scores. Change from mid-2025 to mid-2026 is estimated based on mean change scores. Results: The completion rate was 90.7%; there were 7,752 respondents. As in 2025, high levels of support for and willingness to participate in political violence were uncommon in 2026. Of 53 items addressing anticipation of, justification for, and willingness to commit political violence, 51 showed decreases from 2025 to 2026. All 51 decreases were small, but 35 were significant; only expectation of civil war increased significantly. Decreases from 2025-2026 occurred across the political spectrum. In 2026, MAGA Republicans and MAGA supporters who were non-Republicans were often more supportive of political violence than others, and the latter were often more willing to engage in it. Conclusions: Nearly all measures of support for and willingness to commit political violence decreased for the population as a whole, in many cases across the political spectrum. Higher levels of support for and willingness to participate in violence among MAGA supporters who were non-Republicans warrant further investigation. These findings can help advance prevention efforts, which are urgently needed in this US midterm election year.

title: The Gender Pay Gap and the Child Tax Credit: Credit Eligibility and Unexplained Differences in Mothers’ and Fathers’ Earnings (Working Paper)
abstract: One of the most striking differences in eligibility for the full Child Tax Credit (CTC) is by family type (female and male heads of household and two-parent, married households). Differences in the wages of working mothers and fathers unexplained by key wage predictors can help explain these disparities. This paper explores the interactions between unexplained gender wage gaps and full CTC eligibility using data from the 2025 Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS-ASEC). We examine CTC eligibility across the earned income distribution by family type, estimate how much of the wage gap is unexplained by key wage predictors, simulate counterfactual wages and earnings for all working mothers absent this unexplained gap, and recalculate their families’ CTC. Findings suggest that unexplained differences in the wages of working mothers and fathers leave roughly 1.7 million mothers and 2.9 million children ineligible for the full CTC.

title: Déchets solides ménagers du marché Nkoulouloun à Douala (Cameroun) : caractérisation, gestion et potentialités de valorisation dans une perspective d'économie circulaire
abstract: Municipal solid waste management in urban markets is an environmental, economic and organizational challenge. This study analyses the characteristics of municipal solid waste generated at Nkoulouloun market in Douala II, its management practices and its valorisation potential within a circular economy perspective. A holistic-systemic approach was used, combining a literature review, direct non-participant observations, interviews with stakeholders involved in waste management and valorisation, and a questionnaire survey of 170 traders. Quantitative data were processed through frequencies and percentages using Excel and SPSS. According to data provided by the Douala II municipality, waste generation is estimated at about 50 tonnes per week. Organic waste accounts for 49.6%, plastics and textiles for 37.9%, and metals and other waste for 12.5%. Management involves collection and temporary storage by municipal sanitation staff, followed by evacuation by HYSACAM. However, 59.4% of surveyed traders reported evacuation after two weeks and 40% after three weeks. Nearly 80% reported declining sales associated with poor market sanitation; 66.4% reported damage to commercial property and 33.5% damage to merchandise. Interviews identified potential valorisation pathways for organic, plastic and metal waste, as well as stakeholders who could potentially be involved. The findings indicate that the composition of the waste stream offers valorisation opportunities, while implementation depends on source separation, collection, and infrastructure and stakeholder coordination. Keywords: municipal solid waste; urban market; circular economy; waste valorisation; waste management.

title: Stockholm Syndrome: Origins, Evidence, and Institutional Legitimation
abstract: This article examines whether Stockholm syndrome, a term that emerged from the 1973 Norrmalmstorg bank robbery, is supported by the available evidence. Using primary sources and a review of the literature, it finds that the psychiatrist who pioneered the label never assessed the hostages, that the hostages' behavior may reflect reasonable responses to danger, and that the term followed a hostage's public criticism of how police handled the situation. Drawing a distinction between the cultural reach of Stockholm syndrome and the clinical record behind it, the article explores the consequences of this gap for psychology and its neighboring fields. The term continues to appear in textbooks and applied settings despite this evidentiary gap. Scholarship also suggests that the label has often been applied along gendered lines, including to women whose responses were characterized as irrational. The term's wide circulation may have narrowed what questions get asked about captivity bonding and kept explanations like trauma bonding from receiving consideration. From this, the article develops a broader account it terms circular institutional legitimation, in which a construct gains apparent scientific authority through successive institutional adoptions that substitute for empirical validation.

title: Political Coordination Without a Ruling Party: Informal Networks in Post-Revolutionary Iran
abstract: The Islamic Republic of Iran dissolved its only ruling party in 1987 and has governed its provinces ever since without the organisation that comparative politics treats as essential to durable authoritarian rule. Yet elections have been held continuously, elites have circulated at extraordinary rates---roughly two in three parliamentary incumbents and four in five city councillors are replaced each cycle---and mass participation has persisted, with some 273,000 candidates registering for a single round of local elections. This article asks how political coordination is accomplished at the subnational level in the structural absence of party organisation. Drawing on original electoral data covering all eleven parliamentary terms and on remote qualitative fieldwork in Khuzestan Province, it argues that durable, territorially embedded informal networks---kinship and tribal structures, religious associations, patronage hierarchies, and economic coalitions---perform the coordinating functions normally attributed to ruling parties. Read through Gramsci's account of hegemony and the integral state, these networks constitute decentralised sites of consent production that complement, rather than replace, coercive and institutional power. The case of Dezful illustrates the mechanism. The argument specifies a model of network-based hegemony with implications for the study of authoritarian durability, party substitution, and informal institutions beyond Iran.

title: Revisiting L1-L2 Processing Differences in NPI Licensing: A Maximal Mixed-Effects Approach
abstract: This study reports a re-analysis of deMeurisse and Kaan's (2024) data on L1 transfer effects in negative polarity item (NPI) licensing, employing a maximal mixed-effects modeling framework. Whereas the original investigation relied on a reduced random-effects structure comprising only random intercepts by participants, we applied a more inclusive model that incorporates random slopes for licensing conditions by participants, following recommendations in the literature (Barr et al., 2013). A model comparison demonstrated that the maximal structure yielded a significantly superior fit (ΔAIC = 78.18), while the core L1 transfer effect remained stable under this more stringent analytical approach. These results reinforce the utility of maximal random-effects specifications in experimental psycholinguistics.

title: Naming Violence: Obstetric Suffering, Emotional Communities, and Feminist Political Action in Spain
abstract: This article examines how obstetric experiences came to be named and recognized as violencia obstétrica within the feminist association El Parto es Nuestro (EPEN) in Spain, and how that naming became the foundational act of a sustained political movement. Drawing on feminist ethnography conducted in Madrid between 2023 and 2024, including participant observation, twenty semi-structured interviews, and documentary analysis of the association's fifteen-year digital archive, I argue that naming is not merely descriptive but constitutive: it transforms isolated suffering into a shared grammar of pain, and that grammar becomes the infrastructure of collective feminist action. The article attends to three interrelated dimensions: the embodied transformation through which women move from self-blame to structural critique; the transnational genealogy of the category violencia obstétrica, which traveled from Venezuela and Latin America to Spain and thereby inverts conventional flows of feminist knowledge; and the internal fractures of the movement, which reveal that the emotional community built around obstetric violence is not homogeneous but shot through with inequalities of class, generation, religion, and race. Grounded in feminist anthropology, theories of epistemic injustice, and Myriam Jimeno's work on emotional communities, the article traces the trajectory from bodily dispossession to political subjecthood.

title: Architectures of Denunciation: Feminist Infrastructural Labour, Digital Organising, and the Political Durability of Obstetric Violence
abstract: This article examines how feminist digital infrastructures are organised, maintained, and made politically durable through the case of El Parto es Nuestro (EPEN), a Spanish association contesting obstetric violence. Drawing on feminist digital ethnography, including fourteen months of participant observation, twenty semi-structured interviews, 1,128 blog posts published between 2010 and 2024, the association's website, and seventeen campaigns, I ask how feminist organising becomes sedimented in digital architectures over time. I develop the concept architectures of denunciation to describe socio-technical arrangements through which dispersed experiences of harm are accumulated, classified, retrieved, connected to evidence, and made available for future mobilisation. The article argues that these architectures do not persist through technical affordances alone. Their political durability depends on feminist infrastructural labour: the often invisible work of tagging, maintaining links, preserving screenshots, translating, curating evidence, updating websites, and migrating archives. EPEN's trajectory shows that persistence is an organisational accomplishment rather than an inherent property of digital media. By bringing gendered affordances into dialogue with feminist organisation studies, I show how digital feminist activism is sustained through the interaction of socio-technical possibilities, collective maintenance, organisational memory, and finite volunteer labour. The article contributes to feminist studies of organising by demonstrating that infrastructures are not simply channels for activism but sites where feminist knowledge, memory, and political categories are continually reproduced.

title: Changes in homeownership and entry into parenthood in the Nordic countries
authors: INVEST Flagship, Jessica Nisén, Lars Dommermuth, Sofi Ohlsson-Wijk1, Peter Fallesen
abstract: Since 2010, fertility levels have declined unexpectedly in all Nordic countries, with record lows being reached in recent years. The reasons for these declines are unclear, except that fewer people are becoming parents. The aim of this study was to investigate whether changes in housing tenure played a role in the declined entry into parenthood. We expected that changes in housing tenure, particularly a decline in homeownership related to housing affordability challenges among young adults, may have contributed to this decline. Using harmonized Nordic individual-level register data, we assessed to what extent changes in housing tenure, changes in fertility behavior within tenure groups, or both, contributed to the decline. Discrete-time event history models and multivariate decomposition were applied. According to our results, homeownership among young adults declined in the 2010s in Denmark and Finland – but not in Sweden or Norway. The decline in first births was only partially attributable to compositional change in housing tenure along with other socioeconomic factors in Denmark, Finland and Sweden. Entry into parenthood declined among women, regardless of their tenure status, in all four countries during the 2010s, suggesting the importance of behavioral changes. However, the decline was more pronounced among renters than homeowners.

title: rcrisp: An R package for urban river space delineation
abstract: rcrisp provides tools to automate the morphological delineation of riverside urban areas—i.e., the spaces surrounding a river where social, environmental and economic phenomena are assumed to be influenced by the presence of the river—following a method developed in Forgaci (2018, 88-89). The method is based on the premise that analyses of riverside urban phenomena are often done without a clear and consistent spatial definition of the area of interest and that a morphological delineation—combining the natural terrain of the river valley and the configuration of the overlapping built urban fabric—can provide a more objective and comparable approach. Delineations following this morphological delineation method enable integrated local analyses, where data from different sources must be combined within a neutral spatial unit, as well as global cross-case analyses, which require a spatial unit that is comparable across different geographic contexts. The method proposes a hierarchical delineation of four spatial units: the river valley, the river corridor, the corridor segments, and the river space (i.e., the area between the riverbanks and the first line of buildings). Accordingly, rcrisp includes functions to delineate each, as well as an all-in-one function that runs all desired delineations. The package also includes functions to download and preprocess OpenStreetMap (OSM) and global Digital Elevation Model (DEM) data, which are required as input data for the delineation process. The resulting delineations can be used in any downstream analysis of riverside urban areas that can benefit from consistent and comparable spatial units, including land use, accessibility, and ecosystem services assessments.

title: Communication is not consultation: a documentary analysis of participation depth and the architecture of community engagement during the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
abstract: Introduction: Risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) is treated as essential to Ebola response, but routine reporting can collapse qualitatively different forms of participation into a single category of "engagement." We examined what kinds of participation were actually demonstrable in the documentary record of the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease (BDBV) response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), and what the reporting system itself made visible. Methods: We conducted a documentary analysis of national outbreak SitReps and companion RCCE streams through 3 September 2026. A literature-informed 0--7 framework distinguished no documented interaction, information, sensitisation/mobilisation, feedback collection, consultation, negotiation, iterative participation, and co-design/shared decision-making. Exact source excerpts, actors, dates, sources and validation status were retained. The frozen primary dataset comprised 180 RCCE documentary units; 156 were validated directly to source PDF/text and physical page, and 24 late-window units were verified to the processed national stream pending original-page validation. Results: Thirty units (16.7%) were information, 111 (61.7%) sensitisation/mobilisation, 37 (20.6%) feedback collection, and two (1.1%) consultation. No source-verified unit demonstrated negotiation, iterative participation or co-design/shared decision authority. The response nevertheless possessed a substantial listening apparatus: community concerns included treatment-centre conditions, delayed safe and dignified burials, alert handling, decontamination, medicines, vaccines, clinical trials and body presentation. The documentary chain usually ended at feedback capture, clarification or exchange rather than a traceable decision-to-modification pathway. Conclusion: The 2026 response record documents extensive communication, mobilisation and social listening, but makes community influence over response decisions much less observable. The finding is not that deeper participation did not occur; it is that routine epidemic reporting was better equipped to demonstrate reach and feedback than negotiation, adaptation or shared authority. RCCE monitoring should therefore complement reach metrics with explicit feedback-uptake and decision-trace indicators. Keywords: Bundibugyo virus disease; Ebola; community engagement; participation; RCCE; co-production; social listening; documentary analysis; Democratic Republic of the Congo; epidemic governance

title: The social production of epidemic data: response contestation, institutional disruption and surveillance observability during the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo — a longitudinal documentary analysis
abstract: Introduction: Epidemic surveillance is often represented as a technical pipeline converting cases, contacts, specimens and deaths into data. Sociology of quantification and Ebola social-science research suggest instead that the conditions for observation are socially and institutionally produced. We examine this during the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Methods: We conducted longitudinal documentary analysis and within-case process tracing using Institut National de Santé Publique (INSP) situation reports and operational indicators. Candidate mentions were collapsed into unique episodes; event date was separated from report date; source labels such as 'resistance' were preserved but not treated as explanations; and core classification required a documented consequence for access, investigation, sampling, burial, screening, isolation or reporting. The analytic set was frozen at 1 September 2026; narrative streams were checked through 3 September for carry-forward and resolution. Results: Forty-six unique episodes were retained: 22 core observability events, 22 supporting disruptions without a demonstrated observation loss, and two ambiguous events. Observability was disrupted through heterogeneous mechanisms and actors, including armed-group and protest-related access constraints, community refusal, attacks on burial teams, provider strikes and non-payment, protocol refusal by humanitarian or military personnel, patient escapes, delayed team arrival, and security decisions releasing bodies before sampling. Several episodes documented repair after mediation, payment intervention or security support. Negative cases were informative: some attacks caused injury without a documented missed observation, and one multi-locality report recorded continued safe burials and swabbing despite source-labelled 'resistance'. Conclusion: Epidemic data are relational achievements. Missingness and delay can be endogenous to response relationships and institutions rather than merely technical defects. Treating heterogeneous mechanisms as generic 'community resistance' obscures both causation and correctable response failures. Surveillance systems should preserve structured metadata on non-observation, actor, mechanism and restoration to better distinguish absence of disease from absence of observation. Keywords: Bundibugyo virus disease; Ebola; epidemic intelligence; surveillance; observability; data production; community engagement; health systems; Democratic Republic of the Congo

title: Refugee Return: Theory and Evidence
authors: Ala Alrababah, Marine Casalis, Dominik Hangartner, Daniel Masterson, Jeremy Weinstein
abstract: What explains refugee return? We theorize return as a two-stage process. Safety screens return, and other factors begin to shape who returns only after refugees judge it safe enough. We test this argument with an 11-wave panel of 3,003 Syrian refugee households in Lebanon from 2019 to 2026, spanning the fall of the Assad regime. Before the fall, the return rate averaged 1.6\% per wave despite worsening conditions in Lebanon, and baseline intentions rarely translated into return behavior. After the fall, the rate rose to 9.7\% per wave, while intentions, income, and networks became stronger predictors of return. Event-study estimates show that the increase was concentrated where the regime previously posed the threat: by the last wave, the return rate rose 10.1 percentage points (95\% CI [3.7, 16.5]) more in areas under the new government than under the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces. Qualitative interviews further show how safety shapes return.

title: The Nexus of Voluntary Action and Humanitarian Imperative: A Comprehensive Analysis of Principled Service in Crisis Contexts
abstract: This paper examines the relationship between voluntary action and humanitarian principles within contemporary crisis response frameworks. Drawing upon the foundational principles of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement, particularly Voluntary Service, the analysis explores how volunteerism functions as both an ethical imperative and practical necessity in humanitarian action. Through documentary analysis and case study examination across five contexts—Lebanese Red Cross during civil war, Rohingya refugee camps in Bangladesh, youth volunteer exchange in Nepal, refugee volunteering in Uganda, and British Red Cross operations—the research investigates motivations, institutional frameworks, and impacts of voluntary humanitarian work. The paper argues that voluntary service constitutes an indispensable pillar of humanitarian response, yet faces increasing challenges including securitisation, resource constraints, and tensions between organisational principles and operational realities. The analysis reveals that while voluntary humanitarian action has evolved from wartime medical assistance to encompass comprehensive community resilience and development, its effectiveness remains contingent upon sustained institutional support, principled commitment, and recognition of volunteer agency. The paper concludes by identifying pathways for strengthening voluntary humanitarian action through enhanced partnership frameworks, sustainable funding mechanisms, and greater attention to volunteer wellbeing and motivation.

title: “It’s a soul supplement”: an exploration of microdosing psychedelics through an in-depth interview with a user
abstract: Microdosing consists of the regular use of sub-perceptive doses of psychedelics substances, most notably psilocybin (“magic”) mushrooms and lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD). First observed in specific environments and subcultures before spreading in wider areas of human activity, microdosing has become one of the better recognised faces of the current “psychedelics renaissance.” Building on a body of qualitative research that examines the reasons people engage with substance use, how their practice is embedded in the context of their everyday lives, and the ways these experiences shape them and are vested with meaning, this article draws on an extended, in-depth interview with a microdosing user. Approaching microdosing as a particular use modality of psychedelic substances, a number of interrelated issues are identified and explored in the discussion. These include the multiple, situated and shifting nature of motivations for microdosing, the gradual process of becoming entailed in the practice, the language and values used to express and signify the stance towards and experience of microdosing, the continuum of enhancement and therapy, and the two-way relationship between different use modalities (micro- and macro-dosing) undertaken by the same user.

title: From Menarche to Motherhood: Fertility Patterns by Age at Menarche Across 40 Years in Norway
authors: Kathryn Christine Beck, Øystein Kravdal, Maria Christine Magnus, Jonathan Wörn, Martin Flatø
abstract: Age at menarche marks the onset of reproductive capacity, but its association with fertility has likely changed over time amid secular shifts in both menarcheal timing and fertility behavior. In this study, we examine how menarcheal timing is associated with first-birth timing, childlessness, and completed fertility across 40-years of birth cohorts in Norway using regional health survey data linked to administrative registers for over 60,000 women. Earlier age at menarche was associated with earlier entry into motherhood, although this association weakened in younger cohorts. By contrast, late menarche became increasingly associated with delayed first births and, in younger cohorts, with slightly lower completed fertility. These patterns were not explained by shared family background between siblings or by differences in educational trajectories between menarche groups. The findings suggest that developmental timing may play a larger role in explaining divergence in fertility outcomes, particularly with regards to the timing of childbearing, as family formation has shifted to later ages and life courses have become more individualized. These findings underscore how biological characteristics and social context jointly shape reproductive life courses and the importance of incorporating biological and developmental factors alongside social factors into demographic research on fertility change.

title: Caste-based social exclusion and poverty in Nepal
abstract: This study analyzes caste-based social exclusion and poverty using primary data collected from 448 households in Bheri municipality, Jajarkot district, Nepal, supplemented by secondary data from 34 companies listed on the Nepal Stock Exchange （NEPSE）. The collected data were analyzed using descriptive and econometric models such as the chi-square test, t-test, and binary logistic regression analysis. The study reveals that low-caste people are facing discrimination and social exclusion in accessing quality education and the labor market. These factors negatively affect their livelihoods, resulting in low-quality education, an income gap between upper and lower castes, and overall income inequality. These negative impacts contribute to consumption-based national poverty for low-caste and marginalized households in rural Nepal. Being low caste increases the probability of being poor by 1.533 times, which is statistically significant in less than 5%. Engagement in daily-based labor for their primary income sources will increase those households’ likelihood of being poor by 3.65 times compared to other sources of income, with a significance level of less than 1%. Moreover, having more dependent family members in households and engaging in subsistence farming also significantly contributes to falling into poverty. To enhance the livelihoods of low-caste and marginalized households, the government should prioritize combating poverty by increasing community engagement programs, ensuring equal access to the labor market, and quality education for these communities. Furthermore, private companies should also prioritize combating poverty through providing start-up business funds, job opportunity, and corporate social responsibility initiatives.

title: Bridging Gender Gaps in Information Technology: Women’s Contribution to Economic Growth and Development
abstract: The Information Technology (IT) sector has become one of the major contributors to economic growth, and women are playing an increasingly important role in its development. Women’s contributions have helped companies become more innovative, improve efficiency, and design products that meet the needs of a wider group of users. Hence, it is important to understand how the participation of women in the IT workforce influences innovation, productivity, employment, and overall economic performance. This review article discusses the growth of women's participation in technology, the challenges women continue to face, and the role of government initiatives and corporate policies in creating better opportunities. The study also explores the economic impact of women in the technology sector through case studies of Indra Nooyi, Susan Wojcicki, and Infosys, highlighting how leadership, innovation, and inclusive workplace practices contribute to business success and national development. The observations indicate that greater participation of women in the IT sector not only promotes gender equality but also strengthens innovation, expands employment opportunities, and supports sustainable economic growth. Continued investment in education, digital skills, and inclusive workplace policies will be essential for increasing women's contribution to the future digital economy.

title: Urban Typology is not Destiny: The Succces of the High-Modernist Tower and Slab Public Housing as a Global Outlier in Singapore
abstract: In global urban discourse, the modernist tower-and-slab high-rise is almost universally pathologized as a spectacular failure of top-down social engineering. From Western public housing projects to post-communist concrete blocs, these monoliths are widely viewed as deterministic monuments to alienation and the limits of authoritarian high modernism. This paper challenges that architectural determinism by examining a stark global outlier: Singapore. In the city-state, high-modernist public housing not only survives but thrives, sheltering eighty percent of the population in highly livable, wealth-generating estates. By analyzing this spatial anomaly, this paper argues that the physical reality of the high-rise is not inherently criminogenic or socially isolating. The widespread global decay of this typology was fundamentally a downstream symptom of neoliberal abandonment and the hollowing of the welfare state. Singapore’s exception is sustained by fiercely guarded political-economic conditions: a radical state monopoly on land, the mobilization of captive domestic capital, and an ideological commitment to housing as a perpetual nation-building project. Ultimately, the Singaporean outlier proves that when insulated from market abandonment and continuously adapted to civic metis, the high-modernist high-rise ceases to be a dystopian relic, functioning instead as a highly livevable urban form.

title: 22nd International Review of Leave Policies and Related Research 2026
authors: Ivana Dobrotic, Ásdís Aðalbjörg Arnalds, Gayle Kaufman, Alison Koslowski, Peter Moss, Marie Valentova
abstract: The International Network on Leave Policies and Research has been producing an annual review of leave policies and related research since 2005 (for earlier reviews, go to the network’s website www.leavenetwork.org). The review covers Maternity, Paternity and Parental leaves; leave to care for sick children and other employment-related measures to support working parents; and early childhood education and care policy. The International Review is based on country notes from each participating country, prepared by members of the network and edited by a team of network members. Each country note follows a standard format: details of different types of leave; the relationship between leave policy and early childhood education and care policy; recent policy developments; information on take-up of leave. The International Review also includes definitions of the main types of leave policies; and cross-country comparisons. These comparative overviews cover: each main type of leave; the relationship between leave and ECEC entitlements; and policy changes and developments since the previous review. We also include a technical appendix. The 2026 International Review covers 53 countries. These are: Argentina, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Brazil, Canada, Chile, China, Costa Rica, Colombia, Croatia, Cyprus, Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, Israel, Ireland, Italy, Japan, Korea, Kosovo, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Mexico, Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Russian Federation, Serbia, Slovak Republic, Slovenia, South Africa, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey, United Kingdom, United States of America, Uruguay and Vietnam. Costa Rica is a new country note joining the review this year for the first time. The content of the International Review is to the best of our knowledge correct at the time of going to press, but mistakes may occur. If you should have a query or find an error, we would be grateful if you would contact the country note authors as relevant and the editors. We recommend that readers consult the most recent version of the International Review where possible, as we are unable to retrospectively rectify errors.

title: Early Warning Signals of Sudden Changes in Walking Behavior
authors: Dario Baretta, Alexandre Mazéas, Aïna Chalabaev, Jennifer Inauen, Guillaume Chevance
abstract: Health-protecting behaviors such as walking are crucial for health, yet positive behavior changesare often accompanied by setbacks and relapses. Previous research suggests that critical fluctuations in behavioral time series might foreshadow relapses as early warning signals. This study examines the association between critical fluctuations, quantified as dynamic complexity(DC), and impending sudden changes in walking behavior. We analyzed step count data from 21,425 participants during enrollment in a digital physical activity intervention, covering a total of 5,474,501 person-days. Step counts were recorded via smartphones or wearables. Generalized multilevel models revealed a positive association between DC and impending sudden losses in walking (odds ratios [OR] 1.93 - 1.32). In contrast, the association between DC and impending sudden gains was weaker and less consistent (OR = 1.10 - 0.89). These findings provide evidence for the role of critical fluctuations as early warning signals for sudden losses in walking behaviorand highlight their potential in designing timely and targeted interventions.

title: English-only publishing is a form of brain drain for non-English speaking countries
abstract: By relying solely on English as science’s lingua franca, researchers are disconnecting them-selves from local knowledge systems, thereby diminishing their research impact on their societies and denying their local language the opportunity to grow its scientific lexicon. Over time, this ‘linguistic brain drain’ weakens local journals, marginalizes locally relevant research agendas, and deepens dependence on English-language publishers and indexers that privilege international visibility over local impact. Mitigation requires making modern science more inclusive. Specifically, promoting multilingual scholarly communication must be treated as development policy. Governments, universities, and funders should invest in local publishing infrastructures, reward multilingual outputs, support research addressing local priorities, and reform evaluation systems that undervalue non-English scholarship. Publishers and indexers should implement the UNESCO Recommendation on Open Science and the Helsinki Initiative on Multilingualism in Scholarly Communication. Generative AI, through the use of AI translators, can support multilingual scholarly communication. Challenges and their mitigations are further discussed.

title: Weathering the Ballot Box: Climate Disasters Response and Electoral Behavior in Colombia
abstract: Do voters hold politicians accountable for climate-related disasters? Existing research offers competing explanations: some argue that voters punish incumbents for poor disaster management, others emphasize the electoral rewards of effective relief, and still others highlight contextual conditions—such as disaster timing and intensity—that moderate these effects. This paper develops and tests a conditional accountability framework that integrates these perspectives, arguing that the political consequences of disasters depend jointly on disaster exposure and the credibility of government response. Using a novel dataset of over 47,000 climate-related disasters in Colombia (1998–2021), linked to municipality-level presidential election results, I estimate fixed-effects models capturing within-municipality and within-cycle variation in disaster exposure and relief. The results show that disasters generally reduce incumbent vote share when they are severe or occur close to elections, but that timely and visible relief can partially offset these effects. These findings unify competing theories of disaster politics and show how accountability under climate stress depends on the interaction between citizen evaluation and government strategy.

title: Enhancing motivation through music therapy in subacute stroke rehabilitation: a within-subject crossover study
authors: Theo Dimitriadis, Sjoerd Huisman, Mohammed Mudarris, Dieuwke S. Veldhuijzen, Andrea Evers, Wendy L. Magee, Rebecca Schaefer
abstract: Objective This study examined motivation as a possible working mechanism for music therapy in stroke rehabilitation. We hypothesised that music therapy would lead to increased motivation for rehabilitation and explored its potential association with improvements in motor and/or functional and subjective (measures of) recovery. Methods Using a randomised within-subject crossover design, sixteen subacute stroke survivors received either Neurologic Music Therapy (NMT) plus standard care, followed by standard care only, or vice versa. The NMT intervention consisted of 6-9 half-hour sessions using Therapeutic Instrumental Music Practice and Music in Attention and Concentration Training. Motivation was assessed using the Brain Injury Rehabilitation Trust Motivation Questionnaire, alongside functional motor, cognitive, and quality of life measures. Results and Conclusions Music Therapy significantly increased motivation (p = .041), with an average increase of 8.72 in motivation scores during NMT plus standard care, while showing a 4.43 decrease during standard care alone. No significant association was found between motivation changes and cognitive or motor outcomes. Despite limitations due to missing data, the study suggests that NMT enhances motivation for rehabilitation in the subacute phase after stroke. Larger-scale studies are needed to evaluate the impact of music therapy-related increases in motivation on recovery.

title: Recovering Collective Structure in Congressional Voting: A Fused Latent Factor and Network Approach
abstract: Congressional voting reflects collective behavior structured by chamber-wide patterns such as partisanship and relational patterns among particular subsets of legislators, including factions and coalitions. Yet latent factor frameworks that dominate roll call analysis assume conditional independence across legislators and represent their ideal positions in a linear space. These restrictions can obscure relational patterns that do not align with chamber-wide latent dimensions. To model these behaviors, we adopt a fused latent factor and network model that captures chamber-wide patterns with the latent factors and attributes residual structure to the network. Applying this fused model to the 101st (1989--90) and 114th (2015--16) Senates, we first validate that the latent factors recover partisan voting patterns and identify two systematic failures of the latent factor: senators with moderate latent positions are assigned uncertain probabilities on party-line votes, and intra-party split votes exhibit systematic co-defection patterns. The network component closes the misprediction gap entirely for party-line votes but only partially for intra-party splits, capturing stable co-defection patterns while leaving more transient coalitions less predictable. Next, we apply a degree-corrected stochastic block model to the fitted network and recover interpretable voting blocs in both Senates. The 101st Senate features within-party factions that match historically documented coalitions and are driven by shared issue interests despite overlapping positions in the latent space. In the 114th Senate, the blocks take on an entirely different interpretation, uncovering two institutionally opposed coalitions: a cross-party governing bloc, including members of the Republican party leadership, and a Republican insurgent bloc, both driven by opposition of the other. Our findings demonstrate that roll call data alone contains recoverable signals of collective legislative behavior beyond partisanship that remain after accounting for chamber-wide partisan structure, and the organization of this collective behavior shifts from issue-based coalitions toward institutional conflict across decades of polarization.

title: Towards a demographic analysis of kinship bereavement
abstract: BACKGROUND Kin deaths are universal, but their frequency, timing, and position within family networks vary across demographic regimes. Existing demographic research describes kin loss, but provides limited tools for summarizing its cumulative and life-course consequences. OBJECTIVE We develop a demographic framework to compare bereavement regimes across populations, focusing on three dimensions: cumulative burden, loss of shared lifetime, and generational overlap in kin deaths. METHODS We derive three indicators from age-specific kinship dynamics: bereavement burden, defined from kin-years lived after kin death; shared time lost, measured as expected kin-years of potential coexistence removed by death; and generational overlap, measuring coincidence between age-specific death schedules of different kin types. We apply the framework to female 1950 cohorts in Argentina and Guatemala using UN-2024 data and matrix kinship models. RESULTS The comparison identifies contrasting bereavement regimes. Guatemala has much higher burdens from child and sibling deaths and larger total losses of shared time with these kin. Argentina has a higher grandparent burden and greater shared time lost per child death. Death schedules are also more strongly overlapped in Guatemala, particularly for siblings and parents and for children and parents, whereas Argentina displays a more sequential ordering of losses across generations. CONCLUSIONS Similar death counts can conceal markedly different bereavement experiences. The demographic meaning of loss depends on when deaths occur, how many kin are exposed, and how losses are sequenced across generations. CONTRIBUTION We extend formal kinship demography by providing three interpretable indicators that allow bereavement to be compared systematically across demographic regimes using standard population data.

title: Does belief in supernatural punishment increase prosociality? Evidence from economic games in two religiously pluralistic communities of southern Benin
authors: Augusto Dalla Ragione, Cody T. Ross, Marina Elodie Sedjro Djekinnou, Iranlowo Abakpin Elodie F Lawin, As'Ad Olawale Ichola Assani, Tossou Jeandro Simplice Kakpo, Daniel Major-Smith, Benjamin Grant Purzycki
abstract: The role and durability of religious institutions in human societies has long been the subject of discussion among social scientists. A prominent view in anthropology considers religions-and especially moralistic religions-as institutions that enhance within-group cooperative proclivities and minimize norm violations, by inducing belief in the threat of supernatural punishment and monitoring. This may be particularly important in sustaining cooperation in larger groups, where mechanisms based on kinship, reciprocity, and reputation bookkeeping are less likely to be effective. The empirical literature is mixed, with some standardized cross-cultural studies providing support for claims of a relationship between moralistic punishment/monitoring beliefs and prosociality. For this study, we collected a suite of survey data on sociodemographics and religiosity, and ran economic experiments in two communities in southern Benin, West Africa. The communities are Vodun-majority, with an appreciable presence of Christians. This local religious diversity within the same ecological setting allows us to: (1) study the degree of syncretism between the two traditions, (2) evaluate whether Vodun and Christian believers attribute different levels of moralistic concerns to their respective deities, and (3) address the impact of belief in supernatural punishment on prosociality, as well as test for differences in effects between adherents of the two traditions. Our analyses reveal some statistically reliable associations between measures of religious cognition and experimental behavior, with increased perception of moralistic supernatural punishment being predictive of higher levels of prosociality. Our results, however, are sensitive to how religious cognition is measured, the type of prosocial behavior considered, and the specific religious community under study. We discuss our results within the framework of leading hypotheses on the nexus between religion and prosociality.

title: As duas faces da classe no recrutamento político brasileiro
abstract: Credential and wealth do not necessarily travel together, and they may operate at distinct phases of political recruitment. This article asks at which of them each one selects, entry into candidacy or the ballot box. The evidence is the universe of first-round candidacies registered with the Brazilian Superior Electoral Court between 1998 and 2024, 3.3 million records, whose occupation is turned into a continuous status score through the international classification of occupations, applied to this universe for the first time; occupation, schooling and declared assets for the same person meet from 2006 onwards. The two faces are compared with one another within each stage, never across stages. The correlation between occupational status and declared wealth is 0.195, and lower still among those elected. From the population to the pool of candidates the diploma already separates, by 0.34 of a standard deviation, whereas the ownership threshold does not; net of credential, entry runs mildly against the proprietor. At the ballot box the reading depends on the term of comparison, and against the mass of candidacies capital separates more than credential through owning any assets at all, while within the legal threshold, the minimum vote the law requires to take a seat, the distances shrink without the ordering between the faces changing, the diploma and the value of wealth tied at 0.103 and owning any assets above both, at 0.153. Office by office the faces run along distinct axes, credential following the federative hierarchy and capital the electoral formula, larger in majoritarian races. Class composition within each office barely moved over two decades, even as the share holding a degree nearly doubled. Gender is where the two faces stand furthest apart, because women arrive with more credential and less capital, and their schooling advantage reverses in general elections against the population of their own sex.

title: Posting, Liking, and Messaging: The Correspondence Between Self-Reported and Actual Activities on Instagram and the Role of Question Framing
authors: Frieder Rodewald, Florian Keusch, Szafran, Daria, Ruben Bach
abstract: Research comparing self-reported and actual online behavior has focused primarily on general usage, such as how often individuals visit a platform or how much time they spend on it, and less on on-platform activities such as posting, commenting, or liking. We use respondents' actual behavior on Instagram, obtained through data donation, to examine how self-reports correspond to actual behavior, both for general usage frequency and for six on-platform activities. We test whether the direction of deviations between the two measures varies systematically with how often individuals actually use Instagram and how frequently they engage in each activity. We also test whether question framing affects correspondence for activities in a 2×2 survey experiment that varies the reference period (last seven days vs. typical week) and the response scale (numeric vs. vague quantifier labels). In a pre-registered study based on a probability-based online panel in Germany (n = 428 data donors), we find that self-reports of general usage frequency fall below actual usage for most respondents, and most so among frequent users. For on-platform activities, self-reports match actual behavior more often than they deviate from it, and the direction of deviations varies across activities. Higher actual engagement predicts underreporting for nearly all activities, whereas the association between lower engagement and overreporting is less stable. Contrary to expectations, the reference period does not improve correspondence for any activity, and numeric quantifier labels yield closer correspondence than vague quantifier labels for several activities. We discuss what these patterns imply for what self-reports and digital traces measure, and derive practical guidance for survey design in digital media research.

title: The social structure of metacognition: the role of socioeconomic status and gender on students' self-assessment accuracy
abstract: Educational inequalities are well documented, yet little is known about whether students’ ability to accurately evaluate their own academic performance is itself socially structured. This study examines socioeconomic and gender differences in metacognitive calibration – the alignment between students’ subjective assessments and objective performance – across compulsory schooling in Germany. Drawing on nationally representative data from the German National Educational Panel Study, we analyse mathematics and reading calibration from Grade 1 to Grade 9. Using fractional response models with flexible performance functions, we distinguish overall group differences in miscalibration from differences net of objective competence and examine how these patterns vary across the achievement distribution. Results show that objective competence is by far the strongest predictor of calibration: lower-performing students substantially overestimate their performance, and miscalibration declines with grade level. Raw socioeconomic differences in calibration are consistently observed, but they are largely explained by SES differences in objective achievement. Net SES differences are small and generally attenuate across grades, providing little evidence of an independent socioeconomic gradient in calibration. Gender differences follow a different pattern. In mathematics, girls are better calibrated than boys at comparable levels of competence, with the gap becoming larger in later grades and among higher-performing students. Reading differences are considerably smaller. These findings suggest that metacognitive calibration is strongly anchored in competence, while gendered patterns of self-evaluation may constitute a distinct dimension of educational inequality.

title: For Whom Neighborhoods Matter in Early Childhood: Heterogeneous Effects on Achievement
authors: Nicolai T. Borgen, Henrik Daae Zachrisson, Rosa Cheesman, Torkild Hovde Lyngstad, Eivind Ystrom
abstract: The role of neighborhoods in shaping child and adolescent development is well-documented in empirical research. However, the extent to which neighborhood conditions differentially affect individuals based on their background and individual characteristics remains less explored, particularly during the first decade of life. This paper investigates the heterogeneous effects of neighborhood socioeconomic composition on academic achievement in middle childhood by combining Norwegian administrative data with genetic data from the Norwegian Mother, Father, and Child Cohort Study (MoBa). Employing the Neighborhood Choice Model to address selection bias, we find that exposure to neighborhood disadvantage during a child's first ten years impacts 5th-grade standardized test scores. Furthermore, we find that the impact of neighborhoods varies considerably by socioeconomic background, gender, and children’s load for genetic variants correlated with educational attainment, estimated using within-family genetic variation. Notably, boys, children with a lower polygenic index for educational attainment, and those from families with lower incomes and parental education levels face the strongest neighborhood effects. Conversely, children with a higher polygenic index for education are unaffected by neighborhood disadvantage, as are children with affluent parents. These findings highlight the importance of studying heterogeneous neighborhood effects.

title: What Instagram Records and What Users Report: A Data Donation Study Comparing Digital Traces with Self-Reported Behavior
authors: Frieder Rodewald, Florian Keusch, Szafran, Daria, Ruben Bach
abstract: Understanding how individuals use social media is central to research on its effects, yet most studies rely on self-reports. It remains unclear which behaviors platforms record at all, how closely self-reports correspond to those records, and how question design affects that correspondence. In a data donation study with a German probability-based online panel (N = 531 Instagram users, of whom 121 donated their data), we identified 93 digital traces available in Instagram's data download packages and extracted 49, spanning consumption, engagement, creation, and account management. Prevalence follows a steep gradient: consumption traces such as viewing are near-universal, engagement traces such as liking appear for a majority, creation traces such as posting appear for only a minority, and many specialized features are absent altogether, so several behaviors of potential interest can be studied only within the subgroup performing them. Self-reports correspond reasonably to actual behavior for deliberate, frequent behaviors (e.g., creating stories, liking posts), but poorly for passive consumption and rare behaviors. Experimentally varying the reference period and response format, we find significantly higher correlations under a typical-week framing for one behavior and no significant differences between response formats. We discuss when self-reports may suffice and when donated data is needed.

title: The Dark Side of Legitimation. Experimental Evidence on the Effectiveness of Discursive Strategies Used by Cyber Criminals
authors: Kristina S. Weißmüller, Tijs van den Broek, Alina Kaufmann, Steven James Watson
abstract: Online, criminal organizations regularly use discursive legitimation strategies to influence public opinion about their criminal activities to justify their acts and minimize persecution. Yet, little is known about what types of strategies are effective in the case of criminal organizations. This study addresses this gap by identifying and quantifying how distinct discursive strategies impact citizens’ legitimacy judgment, their attribution of blame for societal harm associated with criminal activity and punitive intent. Using a discrete choice experiment conducted with representative citizen samples in Germany (n=301, Obs.=1,505) and the United Kingdom (n=350, Obs.=1,750), the study shows that distinct strategies can significantly impact citizens’ judgment about the legitimacy of criminal activity, their attribution of responsibility, accountability, and punitive intent. Cognitive and moral legitimation strategies – such as discrediting victims and legitimate institutions, but also signaling transparency and moralizing criminal action – are most effective. Social media amplifies, and higher societal harm reduces the influence of legitimation strategies. These novel insights advance the discourse on organizational legitimacy in the post-factual age of digital communication as well as scholarship on accountability and public opinion on criminal activity, helping practitioners and policy makers understand and counteract legitimation efforts by criminal organizations.

title: Decentralization, Ethnic Fractionalization, and Public Services: Evidence from Kenyan Healthcare
authors: Camille Hémet, Liam Wren-Lewis, Jessica Mahoney
abstract: This paper examines the impact of ethnic fractionalization on public service use by exploiting a major constitutional reform in Kenya. Following an important period of inter-ethnic conflict, responsibility for local health services was decentralized to 47 newly created county governments. Using an event-study design, we find that use of public clinics for births increased significantly after the reform, but only in counties that were relatively ethnically homogeneous. We also find a significant increase in the correlation between county ethnic fractionalization and a range of other measures of public health service use. Services in these counties are also less likely to require payments after decentralization. Using within-county variation to investigate mechanisms, we find healthcare use increases were concentrated among areas and individuals of the same ethnicity as members of the new county government executives. Overall, the results suggest that more ethnically homogeneous sub-national jurisdictions can rapidly increase public service use.

title: Four Kinds of Redundancy: Item Recoverability Across Five Survey Instruments
abstract: Surveys often ask for more than they need to and some answers can be predicted from the other answers in the same questionnaire. This paper develops a measure for how much redundancy a questionnaire contains. Unlike work on shortening psychometric scales, the object here is the whole instrument including questions covering unrelated topics with no common construct. For each item, the measure asks how well that item can be predicted from the rest of the questionnaire, excluding the question block the items belongs to. Predictions come from cross-validated random forests. The measure is a simple skill score, R2 for continuous items and the Brier skill score for categorical ones. Both compare the model against a marginal baseline. This places items of different types, and questionnaires of different lengths, on one scale. The measure is computed from collected responses and requires data from a fielded sample. We apply the measure to five survey instruments. Looking at the most recoverable items shows that recoverability is not one phenomenon. It arises from different sources. It also reveals that few items could be dropped without losing information. The measure is therefore most useful as a diagnostic for questionnaire design.

title: Sequential Structure Without a Linguistic Diagnosis: A Falsification-Oriented Analysis of the Indus Script
abstract: The Indus Valley script remains undeciphered. Under ordinary cross-validated scoring, real Indus sign sequences show a positive trigram-over-bigram predictive gain (the two preceding signs predict the next sign better than one preceding sign alone), replicating closely across two independently extracted digitizations of the same underlying corpus tradition, including the M77 corpus corresponding to the concordance behind the most cited statistical studies of the script (+0.143 and +0.158 bits), and clearing 200-trial null distributions entirely. However, both corpora contain substantial exact-sequence repetition (23 to 33 percent of sequences). When cross-validation folds are constructed so duplicate sequences cannot appear in both training and their own held-out evaluation, the gain reverses sign for both corpora (-0.088, -0.083); when duplicates are instead collapsed to unique sequence types, it weakens to near zero (-0.023, -0.010). A control experiment, grouping sequences of the same size distribution but without duplicate identity, stays strongly positive, ruling out the alternative explanation that this reversal simply reflects smaller effective training sets rather than duplicate identity specifically. This is not a data-handling error, since the repetition is a genuine corpus property, but it means the ordinary-CV result should not be read as established evidence of sequential structure that generalizes to novel sequences, and we treat resolving this as the paper's central open problem. Independently of that question, our most specific test among the mechanisms we examined shows the ordinary-CV gain is not uniquely diagnostic of the particular linguistic generative mechanism we tested, including after rebuilding that generator and a non-linguistic alternative to match the real corpus's own vocabulary and length statistics; neither reproduces the real magnitude in matched or unmatched form. A sample-size curve on two calibration languages shows this estimator rarely returns a positive result below roughly 3,000 sequences for either, evidence against the ordinary-CV result being generic small-sample behavior. We also find evidence against inscriptions being deliberately constructed as globally unique identifiers, though not against more elaborate identifier schemes. The framework, derived corpora where licensing permits, and all experiments are released openly.

title: Breaking the Glass Ceiling: Report on Understanding the Barriers Experienced by People of Colour Academics in the University Sector
authors: Lutfun Nahar Lata, Sara Cheikh-Husain, Derlie Mateo-Babiano, Juliet Rogers, Yajie Li
abstract: The report explores the experiences of racism faced by people of colour (PoC) academics at the University of Melbourne, the University of Sydney, and Charles Darwin University. Within and beyond academia, researchers have discussed how the legacies of colonialism and Eurocentrism continue to shape academic institutions and affect students and staff of colour in distinct ways. While universities are positioned as key actors in fostering inclusive societies, research consistently demonstrates that they also reproduce broader societal inequalities. Within this background, this research investigates the experiences of racism encountered by PoC academics at the University of Melbourne, University of Sydney, and Charles Darwin University. The findings reveal that racism permeates multiple levels of university governance and academic practices. Participants in this research highlighted issues such as the misrecognition and undervaluing of PoC academics’ expertise, institutional racism embedded in university policies and leadership, Eurocentric biases in curriculum, research, and organisational structures, exclusionary funding and publishing practices, and their university’s failure to address these barriers. They also pointed out Islamophobia, anti-Palestinian racism, institutional silence regarding these critical issues; professional isolation, limited professional networks, and disproportionate administrative burdens, particularly affecting migrant PoC academics.

title: From Disaster to Resilience: Developing Smart Settlements in the Himalayas
abstract: Nepal’s catastrophic 26 August 2026 Bhote Koshi–Trishuli flood should be understood not only as a humanitarian tragedy but also as a potentially major turning point in updating national settlement and reconstruction policy. Engineers and scientists have described the floods as a glacier–bedrock collapse that triggered an ice-rock avalanche and debris flow. As per the live updates on September 7, 2026, the total death toll was 1,355, and 4,996 people were missing (The Hindu, 2026). Indian and Nepali rescuers worked urgently to locate and rescue people buried under hydropower tunnels, buildings, mud, and landslide debris. UN News reported on September 3, 2026, that more than 22,000 children in the flood-affected region lacked safe drinking water (UN News, 2026). UNICEF also estimated that at least 19 schools had been damaged and that more than 10,000 school-age children urgently needed safe learning spaces (UN News, 2026). Coming just one year after the July 2025 flood in the same transboundary Lhende–Rasuwagadhi river system, this disaster underscores the risks of rebuilding vulnerable settlements and infrastructure in repeatedly exposed corridors. In the aftermath of this disaster, this article proposes Smart Settlement Guidelines for Nepal, informed by evidence on cryosphere-related hazards and disaster risks that resilient infrastructure, managed relocation, and disaster-resilient building practices can mitigate. Smart settlements should also account for Nepal’s remittance-dependent economy, local and imported food systems, and governance arrangements across local, provincial, and federal levels. Rather than advocating wholesale relocation of affected populations, the article advances a risk-differentiated approach: prohibiting new settlements in scientifically identified high-risk (red) zones, retrofitting viable communities, expanding river and slope buffers, and facilitating voluntary, rights-based relocation where residual risks remain unacceptable. Recognizing that disaster-related destruction does not extinguish property rights, relocation should be underpinned by fair compensation, land swaps, transferable development rights, and livelihood restoration.

title: Emergence is not a phenomenon: Consilience as aspiration rather than metaphysic
abstract: Scientists and philosophers invoke the term “emergence” to justify separations, or to stipulate relationships, between different human explanatory schemes, often held to constitute a hierarchy of scale or detail: physics, chemistry, biology, psychology, economics, sociology. Emergence is used to name or (allegedly) explain the inescapable experience that, though we believe bigger things are made of smaller ones, “higher-order” descriptions of larger things are often dramatically more effective than are attempts to reconstruct them from their constituent parts. This is often taken as a deep epistemological or ontological phenomenon or mystery.
